analysis.one_liner: Taps oil reserves to fight price spikes, taxes oil windfall profits, and raises fuel-economy standards.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Rep. Peter DeFazio with a single cosponsor, the bill was referred to six House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the President release oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve when supply cuts by foreign cartels or oil companies push prices up, require oil companies to hold minimum inventories, and ban exporting Alaskan crude. It would impose a 50% excise tax on oil-company profits above an inflation-adjusted $50 per barrel, ban oil-industry mergers for a year, order a WTO complaint against OPEC, and raise fuel-economy standards for cars and the federal fleet. Buyers of highly efficient cars assembled in the U.S. by union workers could claim a tax credit of up to $6,000. The bill was sent to six House committees and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, farmers, and small businesses paying high gasoline and heating-oil prices would benefit from reserve releases, mandated inventories, and an end to Alaskan crude exports, all aimed at holding prices down. Households buying efficient American-built cars could get up to $6,000 off, and consumers generally would gain if oil mergers were halted and a commission examined why the industry is so concentrated.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and buyers of efficient cars

how_it_helps.text: Expands the President's authority to sell oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve when a price spike harms a state or regional economy or is caused by conduct that lessens competition, and requires a report to Congress when crude exceeds $50 a barrel for two weeks.
Orders the Energy Secretary to set mandatory minimum inventories of crude and petroleum products for producers, refiners, and marketers to limit price swings from supply disruptions.
Repeals the authorization to export Alaskan North Slope oil and reimposes the export ban, keeping that crude in the domestic market.

Imposes a 50% excise tax on integrated oil companies' profits above an inflation-adjusted $50 per barrel, with the tax reduced by investments in refineries and alternative fuel facilities, and sunsets after three years.
Creates a tax credit of up to $6,000 for buying a highly fuel-efficient passenger car assembled in the United States under a collective bargaining agreement.
Bans oil-industry mergers for one year and permanently requires that any petroleum merger be shown likely to benefit consumers by maintaining or increasing competition.
Directs the U.S. Trade Representative to file a WTO complaint against oil-producing countries for coordinated production cutbacks, which the bill calls de facto price fixing.
Raises average fuel-economy standards to at least 37 miles per gallon for cars made after 2017 and 40 after 2022, and requires federal agencies to buy more efficient vehicles.

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies would bear the windfall tax, the merger moratorium, minimum-inventory mandates, and the loss of Alaskan export revenue. Automakers would face higher fuel-economy compliance costs, and the vehicle credit's cost would fall on general taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes the President to issue orders and regulations to stabilize wholesale and retail gasoline prices at set levels, a form of price control that historically risks shortages and misallocation when the set price is out of line with supply costs.

The vehicle credit applies only to cars assembled in the U.S. under a collective bargaining agreement, excluding efficiently built cars from non-union plants, including foreign-owned U.S. factories, and limiting which buyers can actually claim it.

The windfall tax excludes oil from wells drilled after enactment, and it is credited against company investments in drilling, refineries, and alternative fuels, so companies that reinvest heavily could owe little.

Higher fuel-economy mandates raise compliance costs for manufacturers, which can translate into higher sticker prices for buyers, and the bill requires only that standards 'maximize the retention' of auto jobs, a goal that can pull against the efficiency target.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks gasoline prices from several directions at once, and some tools are well aimed: an end to Alaskan crude exports keeps oil at home, a merger moratorium addresses real industry concentration, and the vehicle credit gives consumers money to cut their fuel bills. But the price-stabilization authority is a blunt 1970s-style control that an honest supporter would concede can backfire, the windfall tax's carve-outs make its bite uncertain, and the union-assembly condition turns a consumer credit into a narrower labor-linked benefit. On balance the bill would have traded some economic distortion for real relief at the pump, and it never got far enough for anyone to test that trade in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees and two subcommittees in March 2007; none of them ever reported it out, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on March 13, 2007 with one Democratic cosponsor.

It was referred to six full committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, Natural Resources, and Foreign Affairs — and then to the Energy and Air Quality and Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittees.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the bill at any point in the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies kept their profits untaxed by any windfall levy and faced no merger moratorium, export ban, or inventory mandate; drivers saw no change in pump-price policy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Integrated oil companies avoided new curbs

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Gasoline Price Stabilization Act and spoke for it on the House floor.

for.name: 1 House Democrat cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it attracted no other support in the chamber.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair John Dingell)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; it went to a subcommittee and no hearing or markup was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats put their names on the bill, no Republican supported it, and no vote ever occurred, so no party split was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill taxes 50% of their profits above an inflation-adjusted $50 a barrel, bans their mergers for a year, requires them to hold minimum inventories, and lets the President tap reserves against price spikes they cause. Their gains from high pump prices are the consumers' costs the bill targets.

industries.industry: Alaskan North Slope oil producers and exporters
industries.note: The bill repeals their authorization to export North Slope crude, forcing that oil into the domestic market where it would add supply and put downward pressure on U.S. prices.

Higher fuel-economy standards raise compliance costs, but the bill also creates a credit of up to $6,000 per car for efficient vehicles assembled in the U.S. by union labor, steering demand toward some of their plants. In the end they gained nothing because the bill never moved.
